I'm a mom of 4 kids (ages 12, 11, 6, and 4). They're all fully vaccinated and always up-to-date on regular check-ups. 

My 6-year-old, who I'll call J, is the only kiddo with any issues, and they've generally been mild. He has moderate asthma which is controlled with Flovent, but has otherwise been a healthy and active kid. 

But recently, J has been getting sick a LOT. I just picked up his third prescription for antibiotics in 30 days, and he has had a fever for 6 days now that doesn't completely go away even with multiple fever reducers (it does go down enough that he's comfortable though). Yesterday I noticed he has swollen, bleeding gums and a few ulcer-like sores in the back of his throat which the doctor diagnosed as hand, foot, and mouth disease (no tests were done though). Today I brought him back in due to his fever spiking to 104.6 and him struggling to walk/move last night (also improved - but not completely fixed - with meds) and they did a strep test which came back positive.

The reason I'm really worried though is the weight loss and his medical record in general. I looked up his growth chart when I got home (I can access his records online) and he has grown 1.3 inches in the last 6 months but his weight dropped by 1 pound, causing his BMI to go from the 20th percentile to the 1st. 

I also looked at his blood work. They checked his hemoglobin at his 6-year checkup in July and that was low at 10, but they told me to just make sure he's eating iron (he eats a lot of iron-rich foods but doc said to just increase them). The last time he had a CBC was 5 years ago at his 1 year check-up but I looked at it anyway and his lymphocytes were high and neutrophils were low, but I don't think his doctor ever said anything about abnormal results so maybe that's not a concern? I didn't have online access at the time so I'm sure when they didn't call with results, I assumed they were normal.

Should I have the doctor do a CBC if he keeps getting infections or not gaining weight/losing weight? Or should the doctor tell me if these things are concerning? I feel like a hypochondriac but I really just have a feeling something isn't right. :(

The pain is always present to an acceptable degree but it intensifies when I pronate or flex my wrist, for example. Tennis is typically the kind of sport I can't do anymore because the pain is too intense.

The problem is that the cortisone infiltration (done on the radial extensors) that I did, didn't work. So now, I don't know who to believe and I don't know the cause of my pain. I think that maybe the problem is related to the nerves (radial or medial) and not to the tendons  but that's just a guess.

It is normal to feel some discomfort/pain following abdominal

Talk with your surgeon about how long you will need to take

My 6-year-old, who I'll call J, is the only kiddo with any issues, and they've generally been mild. She has moderate asthma which is controlled with Flovent, but has otherwise been a healthy and active kid.

But recently, J has been getting sick a LOT. I just picked up her third prescription for antibiotics in 30 days, and she has had a fever for 6 days now that doesn't completely go away even with multiple fever reducers (it does go down enough that she's comfortable though). Yesterday I noticed she has swollen, bleeding gums and a few ulcer-like sores in the back of her throat which the doctor diagnosed as hand, foot, and mouth disease (no tests were done though). Today I brought her back in due to her fever spiking to 104.6 and her struggling to walk/move last night (also improved - but not completely fixed - with meds) and they did a strep test which came back positive.

The reason I'm really worried though is the weight loss and her medical record in general. I looked up her growth chart when I got home (I can access her records online) and she has grown 1.3 inches in the last 6 months but her weight dropped by 1 pound, causing her BMI to go from the 20th percentile to the 1st.

I also looked at her blood work. They checked her hemoglobin at her 6-year checkup in July and that was low at 10, but they told me to just make sure she's eating iron (she eats a lot of iron-rich foods but doc said to just increase them). The last time she had a CBC was 5 years ago at her 1 year check-up but I looked at it anyway and her lymphocytes were high and neutrophils were low, but I don't think her doctor ever said anything about abnormal results so maybe that's not a concern? I didn't have online access at the time so I'm sure when they didn't call with results, I assumed they were normal.

A [age]-year-old female with a past medical history of diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, myocardial infarction with stent placement, hypercholesterolemia, migraine headaches, GERD, stroke, bilateral knee arthritis with total knee replacements, and cataract extractions presented with pustular lesions on her buttocks. She reported developing a rash that worsened over time, with associated fever, chills, and right groin pain. The patient denied other symptoms, including headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and dysuria.

Physical examination revealed pustular lesions in the superior gluteal cleft and a hard, tender nodule in the inferior-medial buttock region. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis, anemia, and elevated glucose levels. Microbiology results confirmed Staphylococcus aureus infection, with sensitivities showing resistance to oxacillin and erythromycin. Imaging studies, including a CT pelvis, showed inflammatory stranding consistent with infectious phlegmonous change.

The patient was treated with intravenous vancomycin and ciprofloxacin, and later transitioned to oral clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. Her home medications, including glyburide, metformin, aspirin, carvedilol, and others, were adjusted during her hospital stay. The patient's pain was controlled with hydrocodone-acetaminophen, and she was discharged on a regimen of antibiotics, pain management, and her home medications.

At discharge, the patient's mental status was clear and coherent, level of consciousness was alert and interactive, and activity status was ambulatory and independent. The primary discharge diagnosis was Staphylococcal soft tissue abscess, with secondary diagnoses of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and hypertension. The patient has allergies to Lipitor, Pravachol, penicillins, Percocet, and codeine. Follow-up care was arranged, and the patient was instructed to complete her antibiotic course and manage her pain as directed.

The patient was treated for symptomatic marginal ulcer and was initially kept NPO, then transitioned to a Bariatric stage 3 diet. She received prophylactic subcutaneous heparin and was encouraged to ambulate early. At discharge, the patient was afebrile, hemodynamically stable, tolerating a diet, ambulating, and had well-controlled pain.

The patient has allergies to lisinopril, ketorolac, NSAIDs, and morphine. Discharge medications included oxyCODONE for severe pain, pantoprazole, promethazine for nausea, acetaminophen for mild pain, and continuation of her home medications, including amLODIPine, Atenolol, Buprenorphine-Naloxone, gabapentin, and others.

The patient was discharged home with a diagnosis of marginal ulcer and abdominal pain, and was instructed to follow up as directed. At the time of discharge, her mental status was clear and coherent, level of consciousness was alert and interactive, and activity status was ambulatory and independent.

A ___-year-old male with a history of alcohol abuse presented with a 12-hour history of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He had experienced similar episodes of pain weekly, which resolved with omeprazole. The patient had a history of esophagitis, esophageal tear, arterial hypertension, and a pontine stroke. He denied fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dysuria, and ictericia, but noted urinary frequency. 

Physical examination revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen with tenderness to palpation in the mesogastrium and voluntary guarding. Laboratory results showed elevated alkaline phosphatase (734), AST (60), and glucose (120). Imaging studies, including CT, US, and MRCP, revealed portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis, with marked surrounding abnormal soft tissue and fat stranding. An endoscopic ultrasound did not show a pancreatic mass, but several enlarged lymph nodes were noted in the para-pancreatic region, and a biopsy was taken of the largest lymph node, showing benign-appearing glandular epithelial tissue and lymphocytes consistent with lymph node sampling.

The patient was started on heparin anticoagulation and later transitioned to warfarin. His INR on discharge was 2.6. The patient's nausea and abdominal pain resolved, and he was discharged home on a regular diet with follow-up appointments recommended in the multidisciplinary pancreas clinic and liver clinic. Discharge medications included warfarin, omeprazole, and atenolol. The discharge diagnosis was portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis. 

The patient's condition at discharge was stable, with a clear and coherent mental status, alert and interactive level of consciousness, and ambulatory-independent activity status. Recommendations for further evaluation include a repeat endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy of the excessive soft tissue between the duodenum and the superior mesenteric artery. Allergies: None known.
